asSun.p: Pisces is ruled by Jupiter, with Neptune added by the modern astrologers, and The Moon is Pisces' card among the Majors, so with a Pisces Sun this is the card that comes with the sign. The Sun gets no special help in Pisces. It's a visitor there, and it takes its colour from the sign's rulers, which means Jupiter's generosity and Neptune's blur. That's why a Pisces Sun often doesn't feel much like a Sun to the person who has it. The will is there, it just doesn't march. Pisces is mutable water and the last of the twelve signs, where the zodiac runs out before it starts again at Aries. Look at the path on the card. It climbs out of a pool, runs between two towers, past a dog and a wolf, and off into hills you can't make out, and nobody's put up a sign. A Pisces Sun is usually on that kind of road, and most know it about themselves by fifteen.

Your sense of who you are shifts with the company, and you've probably worried about that more than you needed to. At a work lunch you're funny and a bit dry, at your mum's you're about twelve again, and with a new friend you pick up their turns of phrase within an hour and hear yourself doing it on the drive home. Someone asks what you want for your birthday and you don't know until the week after. Plans you make on a Monday feel like somebody else's by Thursday. An ex may once have told you there was nobody home, and it stung because you'd half wondered yourself. There is. You just take your bearings from feeling, and feeling moves. Jupiter gives the sign a big, forgiving idea of what a person can be, yourself included, which is why you rarely hold last year's version of you against yourself.

You're very good with people at their worst, and it's the gift nobody mentions. The twelfth house is Pisces' natural home, the house of hospitals, retreats and the things kept out of sight, and a Pisces Sun is often the one who can sit in a hospital corridor at two in the morning without needing it to be anything other than what it is. You don't flinch at a mess. A friend tells you something they're ashamed of on a long drive and you just nod and keep your eyes on the road, and they remember that for years. You'll also do good work without needing your name on it, which in most offices is harder to find than talent. Mutable signs adapt, and yours adapts towards whoever's struggling most in the room. It rarely makes it onto a CV, and you'd be the last to put it there.

The shadow people miss is how often you get your own way by going vague. You don't say no to the weekend away, you just never quite book it, and eventually everyone forgets. You agree in the meeting and then do the thing your way, slowly, and it's hard to pin on you. It isn't dishonest exactly. A Pisces Sun hates the moment of saying a hard thing out loud, so the will goes underground and comes back up as drift. The other side is a quiet martyrdom. You give and give, and then there's a small, very private resentment about always being the one who gives, which you'd never say to anyone's face. Virgo sits opposite Pisces, and a bit of Virgo is exactly what you're short of here. Write the date in the calendar. Say no in one plain sentence, on the day it comes up.

When something goes badly wrong, a Pisces Sun disappears. Quietly. You sleep more, you stop answering the group chat, you watch an entire series in two days and couldn't tell anyone what happened in it. After a loss, or a job going bad, the first move is to leave the room in whatever way is available. About a week later you resurface, and you're often kind and capable for everyone else while your own situation sits unopened on the kitchen bench, sometimes literally, letters from the bank included. The people around you worry, and some of them feel shut out, because you were so present for them and now they can't reach you. Usually the thing that gets you moving is one practical person who'll sit beside you while you open the post. Water helps too, a swim, a bath, a walk by the sea.

You fall for potential. You see who someone could be and you love that person, sometimes for years, while the actual one stands there waiting to be noticed. Jupiter makes you generous with belief, so you'll back a partner's plans, the band, the business, the move interstate, long after their own friends have gone quiet about it. That's lovely, and it has a cost. Somewhere along the way your own plans went on hold and nobody noticed, least of all you. A Pisces Sun can build its whole sense of direction around someone else's life and only see how much when it ends. What suits you is a partner who likes that you change from month to month, and who still asks you straight out what you want for dinner and waits for a real answer.

You need work that means something to you, and you need that more than the title. A Pisces Sun in a job that's all targets can do it perfectly well for a while, and then one morning simply can't get out of the car. The fields that tend to suit have some care or some imagination in them, music, nursing, social work, film, counselling, and plenty of Pisces Suns do fine in accounts as long as the people are kind. You're generous with colleagues and hopeless at invoicing, which is Jupiter again. Deadlines are hard. You finish the thing the night before, usually, and it's good. Get someone else, or an app, to hold the dates, and stop treating it as a character flaw that you need one.

At twenty a Pisces Sun is often a bit lost and doesn't mind saying so. Several courses started, a few jobs, long intense friendships, and a lot of time spent being whoever other people needed. The mid-thirties usually bring the first proper boundary, often after something has cost too much, a relationship where you gave yourself away or a job that ran you into the ground. That's when the Pisces Suns who do well start building a small, dull structure around the soft parts of themselves. A routine, a savings account, a friend who says no on your behalf. By the fifties the vagueness has often turned into something close to wisdom, and people bring you the things they can't take anywhere else. The risk at that age is retreat, the twelfth house pulling you further away than is good for you, so keep a few fixed appointments with the outside world.

Once a day this week, before you look at your phone, write one sentence that starts with 'I want'. Skip what you should want, or what would suit everybody, and put down the first honest one. 'I want a quiet evening.' 'I want to leave that job.' 'I want toast.' Don't act on it and don't show anyone. At the end of the week read the seven lines together and see which ones turned up more than once.

asMoon.p: With your Moon in Pisces, The Moon card is yours twice over, which is a bit much, and people with this placement usually laugh when they hear it. The Moon has no special dignity in Pisces. It's a guest there, neither helped nor held back, and it picks up its hosts' habits. Jupiter rules Pisces, so the feelings run large, and Neptune, the modern ruler, means they don't come with hard edges. Pisces is mutable water, the water sign that moves most easily, so your mood tends to match the room, the person, the song on in the car. The Moon itself only shines with light it borrows from the Sun, and you'll probably recognise that. A fair amount of what you feel on any given day, you picked up from somebody else, and you only work out whose it was later.

You absorb. You walk into a friend's flat and know within a minute that they've had a fight with their partner, even though everybody's smiling. A sad film on a Tuesday can colour the whole of Wednesday. A text left on read turns into a complete story in your head by bedtime, usually a sad one, and by the morning you've half forgiven them for something they never did. You cry at adverts and you're slightly embarrassed about it. Sleep matters to you a great deal, and so do dreams, because Pisces belongs to the twelfth house and a lot of your sorting gets done with your eyes closed. After a crowded day, a wedding, a family Christmas, you need a stretch alone with nobody needing anything, or by Monday you're short with people and can't say why.

Forgiveness is the one people miss. A Pisces Moon lets things go, and it's a real ability, the feeling actually washes out of you in a way it doesn't for the fixed signs. Your sister says something cruel at Easter and by winter you've honestly forgotten the words. It makes you easy to live with, too, because a bad mood in you rarely sets hard and nobody has to tiptoe round the house for three days. Then there's what you make out of feeling. The playlist for a friend's breakup, the card you drew for your nan, the song you wrote at nineteen and still know every word of. Jupiter's influence makes the kindness big and a bit indiscriminate, which has its downside, but it means children, old people and nervous strangers tend to trust you on sight.

You let people treat you badly because you can see exactly why they do it. You understand a friend's unkindness so well, the rough childhood, the pressure at work, that you never get round to asking them to stop. Because you take in everyone's feelings, you can also lose track of which ones are yours. You'll be anxious for a week and it turns out to have been your flatmate's anxiety all along. Then there's the escape hatch. A Pisces Moon soothes itself by leaving, into sleep, a screen, sugar, a daydream about moving to the coast, and when things are hard those exits get used a lot. It helps to have one blunt friend who's allowed to tell you when somebody's taking advantage, and to believe them the first time they say it.

Stress goes straight into your body and your sleep. The first thing a Pisces Moon does when life goes wrong is feel all of it at once, and then go numb, and the numb stage can look a lot like calm to anyone watching. A breakup, a death, a bad week at work, and you're very gentle and a bit absent, washing the same dishes twice. A week later the feelings come back in waves, often at odd moments, in the supermarket, in the shower, at a song in a café. The people around you can find it hard, because you're sad in a way that doesn't ask for anything specific, so they don't know what to offer. Rhythm is what gets you through it. Regular meals, the same bedtime, and one person who checks in every day without needing a reply.

You need to feel emotionally met, and you know within a date or two whether that's possible with someone. The catch is that you can feel met by people who are only mirroring you back, because you're very easy to mirror. A Pisces Moon falls for tenderness and now and then gets taken in by it. Pisces trines Cancer and Scorpio, the other water signs, so people with those placements tend to feel like home, and often they are. What's less obvious is that you need a partner who can sit with your moods without taking them personally. You'll be low on a Sunday for no reason at all, and a good partner makes you tea and leaves you to it. A bad one asks what they did. Tell them early that sometimes the answer is nothing, and that it passes.

Your mood is your productivity, more or less, and it's worth building your working life around that. Open-plan offices, constant calls, a manager who sighs a lot, all of it soaks into you, and by Friday you're wrung out without having done anything difficult. You work best with some quiet and some say over your hours. You're excellent at the emotional side of any job, the patient who's frightened, the customer whose complaint is really about something else, the new hire who's struggling and hasn't said so. Colleagues bring you their troubles, often at the expense of your own work. It helps to have a door, even just a pair of headphones, that means leave me be. Choosing between jobs, sit in each workplace for ten minutes if they'll let you. Your body usually knows by then whether you could stand it five days a week.

In your twenties a Pisces Moon usually feels too much and has no idea what to do with it. You take on friends' crises, fall hard for the wrong people, and go out a lot to avoid being alone with your own head. The thirties tend to be where you learn that the moods have a pattern. You notice you crash after big social weekends, or around certain family anniversaries, and you start planning round it. That's usually when the nightly glass of wine, or the scrolling till one, gets an honest look. The fifties bring a softer, steadier version. The feelings are still big, but you trust them to pass, and you've usually made a home quiet enough to recover in. Nieces, grandchildren and young colleagues find you easy to talk to. Keep saying yes to the odd invitation that makes you a bit nervous.

When a strong mood arrives out of nowhere, before you do anything else, ask one question, out loud or in your head. 'Is this mine?' Then go back over the last few hours. Who did you talk to, what did you read, what was on the news, who was sitting next to you on the bus. Quite often you'll find where it came from, and the mood loosens a little once you have. Try it three times this week.

asRising.p: Pisces was coming up over the eastern horizon when you were born, and whatever sign is doing that sets the first house, the body, the manner, the way you start things. So Jupiter rules your whole chart, or Neptune if you go with the modern rulers, and The Moon is the card people meet first. Pisces is mutable water, and at the front of a chart that tends to mean a face that changes with the light. The moon on the card has a face too, but it's only half turned towards you, and a Pisces Ascendant gives strangers about that much. People describe you in completely different ways afterwards, and they're all partly right. Wherever Jupiter sits in your chart is worth finding out, because it says a lot about where your life gets steered.

It's mostly in the eyes and the manner. Pisces rising often has a soft, slightly unfocused look, as if you're listening to something just behind the conversation, and strangers find that either restful or unnerving. People tell you their life story on trains. A shop assistant you've never met tells you about their divorce while wrapping your parcel. At a party you end up in the kitchen with whoever's upset, having arrived meaning to talk to someone else entirely. Asked where you're from and what you do, you give an answer that's true and tells them almost nothing. The people who get as far as your front room are often surprised by how loud it is, books everywhere, two conversations going at once, because Gemini sits on your fourth house of home and life behind the front door is far chattier than your face lets on.

You're very hard to dislike on first meeting, because there's nothing to push against. Someone arrives at a meeting ready for a fight, and you're so open and unguarded that the fight has nowhere to land. Jupiter as chart ruler adds a kind of luck to it, which I've seen often enough to believe in. Pisces rising people get the second chance, the spare ticket, the room upgrade, the benefit of the doubt at the airport. You also pick up on a place before you can say why. You know a flat is wrong the second you walk in for the inspection, and you're right, and the damp shows up three months later. You tend to talk yourself out of that instinct, and with buildings and bosses especially, it's usually worth listening to.

You can end up playing whatever part people have written for you. The partner who needs you to be the gentle one, the boss who's decided you're the creative, the friend who thinks you're fragile, and you go along with each of them to keep the peace. Before long there are five of you and nobody has asked any of them what they want. First impressions cut the other way too. A Pisces rising can look vague in an interview while being quite sharp, and people underestimate you, and you let them because correcting it feels rude. There's a slippery streak as well. You'll give a hazy yes to get out of a conversation, the other person holds you to it, and you're surprised, really surprised, that they heard a promise.

Your first instinct under pressure is to go soft. Someone confronts you in the corridor and you agree with them, apologise and leave, and only once you're in the car do you realise you didn't agree at all. In a real crisis you're often surprisingly good, calm and kind, but it's a calm with nobody quite behind it, as if you're watching yourself from across the room. A week later your body catches up. Bad sleep, a cold, a lot of time staring out of windows. The people around you often had no idea anything was wrong, because your face gave nothing away, and they can feel a little fooled when they find out. Getting somewhere with a long view helps, a hill, a big park, the top level of a car park if that's all there is. So does talking to one person who knew you before any of it started.

With Pisces rising, Virgo sits on your seventh house, the house of partners, and that's a real pull in your chart. You tend to be drawn to people who are exact, practical and a bit anxious, the ones who notice the typo in your email and fix the wobbly chair without being asked. They keep you on the ground, and they often find you a relief after a day of being careful. Early on, a lot of people fall for the mystery and then get frustrated when they can't find the bottom of it. On early dates your instinct is to agree with everything, the film, the wine, their take on their ex, and it's charming for about a month. So let the second date be ordinary on purpose. Say what you actually thought of the restaurant, even if the answer is that it was only fine.

Sagittarius falls on your tenth house, career and public standing, and Jupiter rules it, so the planet that rules your chart also rules your working life. Work tends to go best when it's broad, with travel or teaching or publishing or some big idea behind it, and room to roam a little inside the role. Half the jobs you've had, you probably wandered into sideways. People hire you on instinct. You interview well in a quiet way, you listen harder than the other candidates, and the panel leave feeling understood. Once you're in, the risk is being read as the nice one and passed over for the hard calls. When the difficult client or the messy restructure comes up, ask for it out loud, before somebody decides you're too gentle for it.

Pisces rising at twenty often looks younger than it is and gets treated that way. People mother you, take advantage of you a little, and tell you all their secrets. You're finding out that the face you lead with works like a blank screen, and people draw on it. Through the thirties most Pisces risings learn to give strangers something firmer to go on. Clearer clothes, a firmer handshake, the habit of saying what you think before somebody decides it for you. The Sagittarius tenth house often opens up in that decade as well, a bigger job or a move overseas. By the fifties the face usually settles into something distinctive, warm and a little faraway, and people describe you as calming. Now and then someone still takes you for a pushover, and by that age most Pisces risings quite enjoy putting them right.

In the first five minutes of any new meeting this week, say one thing that's specific to you. A preference, an opinion, a small fact nobody would guess. 'I can't stand coriander.' 'I think the second option's better.' It doesn't much matter what. You want the other person to leave with something about you they didn't have to make up. Then notice who remembers it the next time you see them.

asBirthCard.p: Your birth card comes from the date and nothing else. Add up every digit of your birthday, and if the total's over 22 add those digits again. Yours lands on 18, which is The Moon. That says nothing about where your planets are, and you could be a Capricorn with no water in the chart at all. The card's own astrology is Pisces, mutable water, and as a pattern in a life that tends to mean a path that keeps changing shape under you. Eighteen sits between The Star and The Sun. The Star is hope after a disaster, The Sun is plain daylight, and The Moon is the night walk in between, when you've been given a reason to keep going but can't see properly yet. Add the one and the eight and you get nine, The Hermit, out on his own at night with a lantern. He's the card of Virgo, the sign opposite Pisces, so there's a careful, checking streak folded into the number as well.

As a pattern across a life, eighteen tends to put you in the in-between places. The year after school when nobody knows what you're doing. The six months between leaving one job and knowing whether the next one's real. The long stretch after a breakup where you're not sad any more but not anywhere yet either. Most people rush through those. You seem to keep ending up in them, and you do a lot of your real growing there. You're probably also someone who gets a strong feeling about a situation well before there's evidence, the job offer that's slightly too good, the friend who's about to pull away, and you've been told you're imagining things often enough to half believe it. Then it happens and nobody remembers you said so.

The less obvious gift of eighteen is patience with not knowing. Most people panic when a situation won't resolve. They force the conversation, sell the car, quit the job, anything to get an answer. You can wait. You can live with a test result being unclear for a month, or a relationship being undefined for half a year, without making it worse. In a crisis that's extremely useful, because you're the one who doesn't make the hasty call at the hospital or in the redundancy meeting. You also read what's under the surface of a group. At a family dinner you know who isn't speaking to whom before the mains arrive. People with this card often end up in work that uses that, and they don't always notice they chose it.

Eighteen can get very comfortable in the dim light and then quietly prefer it. Clarity means decisions, and decisions mean losing some options, so you keep things undefined on purpose. You don't look at the balance. You don't ask where the relationship is going. You tell yourself you're waiting for a sign, and the sign would turn up within a week if you asked the question. There's a secrecy streak too. People with this card often keep one part of their life in a separate box, the real feelings about a parent, a debt, a hope they've never said aloud, and the people closest to them are surprised years later when it comes out. It's rarely anything terrible. What hurts them is finding out how long you carried it on your own.

When life goes wrong, eighteen tends to go foggy first. You can't concentrate, you lose your keys, you forget the call you promised to make. It feels like the ground's gone soft. Then the imagination starts up, and at three in the morning every possible disaster gets a full rehearsal. A week later you're usually functioning again, but you've often made one private decision in the dark that nobody else knows about, to leave, to stay, to stop talking to someone. That's hard on the people around you, because they're still reacting to the first week while you've already moved. Daylight helps, in the most literal sense. Get up early, go outside, and say the fear out loud to somebody in the afternoon, when it usually sounds a good deal smaller than it did at three.

In relationships eighteen tends to arrive through a period of not knowing. A lot of people with this card say their big loves started ambiguously, a friendship that turned into something else, months of not being sure what the other one felt. You're comfortable in that stage, possibly too comfortable. The pattern also gives you a sharp sense for when something's off, and the trick is telling that apart from ordinary insecurity. Your partner comes home quiet and you've got a whole theory by the time they've taken their shoes off. Ask before you build the theory. The partners who suit this card are the straightforward ones who say what they mean and don't mind being asked twice, because the reassurance you need is usually one plain sentence.

Across a working life, eighteen usually doesn't take the straight road. People with this card often change fields at least once, or find their real job by accident on the way to another one. You work well where the answers aren't clear yet, research, early projects, therapy, investigations, creative work, anything where you have to feel around for a while before the shape shows. You struggle where every week looks the same and every question has a form. You also tend to know a company's in trouble before the announcement, and it's worth acting on that. What trips you up is not asking for clarity when you're entitled to it. Get the pay, the title and the job description in writing, because left to yourself you'd let them stay vague.

In your twenties eighteen often shows up as a stretch of genuine confusion. Not knowing what to study, drifting between cities or partners, strong feelings with no map for them. From outside it can look like wasted time. It usually isn't. By the mid-thirties the pattern has come round a few times, and you start to recognise the fog as a phase with a far side. You stop panicking in it, and you notice that the decisions you made in those unclear stretches were often the right ones. The fifties tend to bring a quiet sort of authority. People bring you their uncertain situations because you've been through so many of your own. The Sun comes after The Moon in the Majors, and plenty of eighteens tell me the later decades have been the easiest stretch so far.

Keep a notebook by the bed and write one line whenever you wake with a strong feeling or a vivid dream. Just the date and a few words. Once a month, read back through it and mark any that turned out to mean something, a worry that came true, a hunch about a person, a dream that pointed at a real problem. After a few months you've got your own record of when your instinct was worth listening to, and when it was just a bad night's sleep.
